name: Organizational Challenges
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why Competitors Don't Share Well: The Barriers Blockchain Can't Code Away
lesson.summary: The hardest problems in enterprise blockchain adoption are rarely cryptographic; they are competitive distrust, cost allocation disputes, legacy integration debt, and misaligned incentives that no smart contract can resolve on its own.
lesson.body:
By this point in the course, a pattern should be visible: chapter after chapter on the technical side of blockchain, consensus, cryptography, smart contracts, has a mirror-image chapter on the organizational side. That mirroring is not a coincidence. Most well-documented failures of enterprise blockchain projects trace back to organizational barriers rather than technical ones, and this chapter pulls together the recurring shapes those barriers take, building on both consortium governance and stakeholder buy-in.

The first and most distinctive barrier is co-opetition: a consortium blockchain often requires direct competitors to cooperate on shared infrastructure while continuing to compete everywhere else. A shipping line asked to route data through a platform partly owned by a rival carrier is being asked to trust that its competitor will not gain an information advantage from the arrangement, a trust that a technically airtight permissioning system does not automatically create, because the anxiety is about governance and incentives, not encryption. This is the same organizational dynamic that undercut TradeLens, described in the consortium governance chapter, and it recurs across industries wherever a blockchain consortium's most natural members are also each other's competitors.

A second barrier is data sensitivity that goes beyond what the technology can address. Even with strong access controls, participants worry that patterns visible on a shared ledger, transaction volumes, timing, counterparties, reveal competitive intelligence even when the underlying values are encrypted or hidden. A third is cost allocation: someone has to pay for shared infrastructure, and consortium members with different transaction volumes, different levels of benefit, and different appetites for risk rarely agree easily on a formula, especially before the system has proven its value. A fourth is the integration debt hiding inside every established organization's legacy systems; a blockchain component rarely replaces an enterprise's core systems, it has to be bolted onto decades-old databases and workflows, and that integration work is often larger, slower, and more expensive than the blockchain component itself.

A fifth barrier worth naming directly is the skills gap and the incentive misalignment it creates. The team that has to operate and maintain a blockchain system long after launch is rarely the team that championed and built it, and if that operating team was not brought into the buy-in process described in the previous chapter, the system can be technically live and organizationally orphaned at the same time. None of these five barriers, competitive distrust, data sensitivity, cost allocation, legacy integration debt, and operational skills gaps, are fixed by a better consensus algorithm. They are the reason this course spends as much time on governance, change management, and stakeholder buy-in as it does on hashing and consensus: a blockchain project's odds of success are set as much by whether the organizations involved can actually cooperate as by whether the code compiles.
